# Week 36, 2026

Highlights selected from everything kept between August 28, 2026 and September 4, 2026. Items are selected several times a day by an automated pipeline and the summaries are machine generated; follow the links to the original sources. See [About](../../about.md) for how selection works.

<img class="section-banner" src="../../../assets/section-digest.svg" alt="">

## The week in brief

<div class="section-brief">
<p>Two evaluations published in npj Digital Medicine point in opposite directions. On 24 official German medical licensing examinations covering 7485 items, proprietary frontier models scored near ceiling, Gemini 3.1 Pro reached 99.31% on the first examination, and even compact open-weight models exceeded mean student performance <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03082-7">[4]</a>. On the Bones and Joints benchmark, 1245 questions drawn from real orthopedic and sports medicine cases, models exceeded 90% on structured multiple-choice items but scarcely reached 60% on open-ended tasks requiring image interpretation, with frequent text-driven hallucinations, and medical-specific models showed no consistent advantage over general-purpose ones <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03191-3">[3]</a>. Both papers identify image-present items as the point where model performance drops most sharply <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03082-7">[4]</a> <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03191-3">[3]</a>.</p>
<p>For faculty, saturated multiple-choice performance raises the question of what a written exam now measures, which the Oxford AI Competency Centre episode addresses in terms of authorship and academic integrity <a href="https://aipodcast.education/inside-oxfords-ai-competency-centre-rethinking-assessment-and-authorship">[13]</a>. Bedside evidence is similarly mixed: a meta-analysis of 53 sepsis prediction studies found a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88 but a positive predictive value of 34.2%, extreme heterogeneity, and no demonstrated improvement in patient outcomes <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03168-2">[5]</a>. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is nonetheless allowing four generative artificial intelligence (AI) devices, including products from Cadence and Limbic, to reach patients through its TEMPO pilot before marketing authorization <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/09/03/tempo-fda-pilor-generative-ai-medical-device-regulation">[7]</a>.</p>
<p>The vendor releases behind these results continued: OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1QNsdr-Qx_I">[9]</a> and Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROF2Nv_KjOM">[10]</a>, reporting 52.6% on the new Terminal-Bench-Science benchmark, up from 24.7% for Fable 5 <a href="https://simonwillison.net/2026/Sep/1/claude-fable-5-1">[2]</a>. Astra&#x27;s 99.9% score on ARC-AGI 3 was achieved with OpenAI&#x27;s custom harness, while the default harness scored 62.7% <a href="https://simonwillison.net/2026/Sep/3/gpt6-astra">[1]</a>.</p>
<p class="section-brief-date">Written from the items highlighted below; numbered links go to the sources.</p>
</div>
